newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU, Nordics seen moving closer in alcohol talks.
newsitem.headline: EU, Nordics seen moving closer in alcohol talks.

text.p: The European Commission said on Monday there was progress in sensitive talks on phasing out rules that allow the three Nordic EU members to limit the alcohol people may bring back home from elsewhere in the bloc.
"I saw some signs of movement in their position," European Union Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti told reporters at an EU finance ministers meeting in Luxembourg.
He met with Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto and Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved on the sidelines of the meeting.
However, Asbrink said there was still disagreement on the controversial issue. "We've had an exchange of views and we are not in agreement," he told reporters after the meeting.
A new meeting will be held on Wednesday next week, probably in Strasbourg. But it was uncertain whether the same ministers and Monti would attend also that meeting.
Asbrink said there were hopes of an agreement then. "But is far from certain," he added. "It is clear that we meet because we still believe there is a possibility to find agreement."
Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said earlier this month that Sweden, Finland and Denmark want to keep their restrictions on personal alcohol imports unchanged until at least 1999.
However, such a position would be unlikely to go down well with Monti, who is pushing for a fixed date when the Nordics' special import restrictions should end altogether.
"On the date I stressed once again the need to have one," Monti said.

Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict imports of cheaper alcohol, but these will expire by the end of 1996 unless there is a new agreement -- at least according to the Commission.

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they go against the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while the Nordics want to keep them because of health- and tax-reasons.

The issue is politically sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking. It is also a question of fiscal importance as the taxes bring in much needed revenue

A compromise leading to a phasing out of the restrictions would gradually allow Swedes, Finns and Danes to bring in more alcohol while at the same giving the three Nordics time to prepare for the new rules, according to the Commission.
But as Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict imports.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer, much less than most other EU citizens.
